utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Milosevic, it's for you to cross-examine this witness. You have the standard 45 minutes, if you require it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. Before I move on to my questions, I would like us to view the witness's tape that I received as well. It's your tape, isn't it? I gave it to the technical booth. Could it please be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll play it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "JACKY ROWLAND: ... people have been killed in this first wave of bombing, but that wasn't the end of the story. The drone of bombers could still be heard overhead and as we raced away from the scene, NATO struck again. There was clearly no mistake about the target. A narrow escape for us, but maybe not for the prison guards we were speaking to earlier. "Jacky Rowland, BBC News, Istok in Kosovo." "Another NATO bomber drops its payload. The target this time a prison in a remote part of North-western Kosovo. We took these pictures as we fled the scene. Just moments earlier, we were at the prison, inspecting damage from a first wave of bombing. NATO pounded the gaol for two hours in the morning, firing about 15 missiles into the main complex and blowing a hole in the perimeter wall. "INVESTIGATING JUDGE: This is the second time NATO has attacked this gaol. I can't find words to describe what I think. "JACKY ROWLAND: Serb officials insist this was a civilian target. They say the prison houses convicted thieves, rapists and other criminals, but what makes Istok gaol interesting is that among its inmates are members of the Kosovo Liberation Army. "The authorities say a thousand prisoners are being held here. The inmates have been let out of their cells. You can see them behind me, lined up against a wall. Some of them have been killed in the NATO attack. Others may have escaped. By unlocking the cells, the guards thought they'd give the prisoners a better chance of survival. For many, this gamble didn't pay off. Prison officials say at least 19 people were killed in the two waves of bombing today. "The regional capital, Pristina, has also felt the effects of NATO's campaign, although much earlier. This damage in the centre of the city was caused weeks ago. By now, the people of Pristina are falling into the uneasy routine of being bombed and they're trying to get on with their lives. "These people are Kosovo Albanians. They're queuing for new identity documents from the Serb authorities. So while refugees leaving Kosovo have had their papers destroyed, here other Albanians are having new ones issued. "This man says he came to Pristina after fleeing his village. He says he feels safe here and plans to stay. Nevertheless, some Albanians are still leaving Kosovo. These people are heading for the Macedonian border. Some of them have valid documents. Others hope to get through on old passports." "Jacky Rowland, BBC News, Pristina."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That is sufficient. Actually, this entire report, as you can see, you made it round the end of May, as far as I can see, because Pristina follows the events in Istok; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Kosovo for the latter part of May in 1999, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you because what you presented at the end of May -- actually, then you refer to the normalisation of life in Pristina. The end of May was the end of the war, and for six months now we have been hearing witnesses here who have been saying that in Pristina in May, some kind of wild Serb police was going around, killing people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know by now that you can't put to this witness what other witnesses have said. She won't know about that. You could put to her what she saw or heard herself. Now, if you want to put that things were normal in Pristina in May, if that's your question, put it directly rather than interspersing it with comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Rowland, on this footage of yours, no police can be seen whatsoever that is forcing people onto buses with rifles, that is deporting people, beating people, chasing them in the streets. I see that the streets are full; right? So what was your impression? Was your impression the same as you presented it in your report? People are sitting, talking, strolling about in the streets. Some are travelling. Others are waiting for new passports. Is that the way it was or is that not the way it was?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, Mr. Milosevic, I don't think that police officers, if they are going to beat people or chase them out of their homes, they don't generally do it in full view of television cameras.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this report of yours, you use the phrase "Serb authorities." I assume that "authorities" in any territory means the government. Do you know, since at that time you were in Pristina, that the government of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, the provisional government that was appointed by the Assembly of Serbia, consisted of Albanians, Serbs, Turks, Muslims, Roma, Egyptians; that is to say, all ethnic groups that live in Kosovo, and that in that government Serbs were a minority? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for a start, Mr. Milosevic, I don't think it's strictly correct to say it was the autonomous province of Kosovo in 1999 because you revoked that status of the province some years before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not debate that. What you call abolition is in the constitution of Serbia, and when you say that the province was abolished, it does say in the constitution that there is an autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija and also an autonomous province of Vojvodina and these are forms of autonomy. This explanation that says that it was abolished is part of this false indictment. But now let's go back to Istok. Since the beginning of this operation which is called, inappropriately, a trial, did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've had enough comment. Now, you either ask proper questions or you're going to be stopped altogether. Now, have you any questions for this witness, as opposed to making comments as you go along?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I do have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just ask them, and briefly. We'll all get on more quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've given me 45 minutes, very generously, so do let me use them the way I think is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will be stopped -- you will be stopped if you do not act in accordance with the rules. It's as simple as that and you know it. Now, get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity, Ms. Rowland, to see the introductory remarks made by this false Prosecution about the events in the prison in Dubrava where the Serb authorities were blamed, accused of what you actually recorded here, what you saw there. That is to say in terms of the consequences of the NATO strikes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... what the Prosecution said. It's not for this witness. It's nothing to do with her. Now, ask her about what she saw and heard. You've been told that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm asking her. That's precisely what I'm asking her, whether she saw on her very own television a transmission of what was said here about this event that she had reported on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, you're not cross-examining, you're simply making speeches. Now, unless you ask this witness about what she saw and heard herself, as opposed to trying to comment on the Prosecution, you're going to be stopped altogether. Now, have you any questions as to the witness? Not about the Prosecution but about her evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, now we've seen this footage, and I see that you have commented upon that in your statement, that is to say the events in the prison in Istok, why is it significant that you saw a man in civilian clothes, probably a policeman in civilian clothes, who was promenading along the path within the prison and that he has a rifle? What makes this observation relevant at all and what is unnatural about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What do you mean? What do you mean? You must make yourself clear, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is mentioned by way of some kind of proof that something irregular is being done. The fact that there is a policeman who was patrolling up and down a path within the prison is wearing civilian clothes. What does that have to do with anything? Why is this relevant at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us rephrase that so it makes some sense. Was there any significance, as far as you could see, in the policeman wearing civilian clothes? And I guess it's the one who had the rifle and a pistol that's being referred to. Could you see any significance in that, Ms. Rowland, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be in no position as to know whether this man was a policeman or not a policeman. He was a man dressed in civilian clothes, carrying two weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you made this report - this was during your second visit - the prison had already been evacuated; right?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incorrect. The report which shows the man dressed in civilian clothes, carrying the weapons, that was on my first visit to the prison, on Friday, the 21st of May, 1999, not my second visit to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But during your second visit - it doesn't matter whether it's that or something else that you recorded - the prison had already been evacuated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my second visit to the prison, the prison appeared to be deserted, and the officials, the Serb officials at the prison, told us that the prison had been evacuated earlier that day, that day being Monday, the 24th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We saw at the very beginning of this tape which was just played a few minutes ago that cameramen, TV crews, are running, perhaps members of your own crew, I don't know who was all there. So the bombing took place, once again, as you were reporting from the prison; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that during your second visit, you saw on the ground in some places around the prison there were still bodies lying around there that you had noticed during your first visit. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my assumption that at least some of the bodies I saw lying around the grounds of the prison covered by blankets were still those same bodies from the first time that were still lying in situ. Of course, I cannot say for certain whether they were new bodies. It was my assumption that these were bodies from the first bombing, still lying in position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the investigation that was conducted by the investigating judge in charge and the team of the investigating judge from the District Court in Pec was interrupted due to the bombing and that this investigation took place for a few days with a few short interruptions?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, bearing in mind that I saw the investigating judge during my second visit to the prison, all I can know for certain is that this gentleman clearly visited the prison on at least two occasions, the two occasions when I saw him and filmed him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So you assume that until an investigation is over, that part of the scene where the investigating team had not been should remain as it was during the event concerned, that is to say, during the bombing. Did it occur to you that what you saw - that some of the bodies were in the same position as they had been a few days prior to that - was because the judge had not processed certain points yet during his investigation? He had not taken care of certain things, of certain individuals. Or do you think there was some other reason? Isn't it logical for it to be that way while an investigation is going on?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we are to be -- if we're to speak strictly about how investigations would be carried out, one could argue that it was inappropriate for the judge and his team to allow a bunch of international journalists to run around the site of the prison. Normally in an investigation, police officers would wish to keep the scene of the event intact. So the very fact that they allowed us to run around with cameras, possibly damaging evidence, suggests to me that they were not clearly following all the procedures that one would normally expect to be carried out if it's a scene that's under police investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The scene, as we could have established, was under investigation for a few days. Do you hold it against them that they allowed you to come in and to film and to see what it was all about and in this way disrupt the investigation?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does anyone really care whether I hold it against them or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I see that you are addressing critical remarks in respect of the fact that they allowed you to come and film. Tell me, please, is this your article? It says here [In English]: "Tuesday, May 18, 1999, published at 2123 GMT, 2223 UK, by Jacky Rowland in Pristina." [Interpretation] I'm going to read it out to you and then I'm going to put some questions to you in relation to this. [Previous translation continues]... Albanian refugees --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, let's establish where it's from and whether the witness recognises it. Where do you get it from, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I precisely wish to establish whether the witness recognises this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where do you say it appeared so that she may have some idea whether she can recognise it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were not listening carefully. I said Tuesday the 18th of May, 1999, 2123 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Listen to the question: Where did it appear? In what publication are you saying it appeared?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to the best of my understanding, Ms. Rowland is a BBC journalist, so it appeared on the BBC. So I'm asking her whether it's her article and I'm reading it out to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What you're saying is this, as I understand it: It was on the BBC website. Is that where you got it from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was published, Mr. May. That is to say it was released on the BBC on the 18th of May, 1999. I have the actual text. I haven't got the tape, the footage. So I wish to ask her --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Read it and read it slowly, bearing in mind the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. It says by Jacky Rowland in Pristina, Kosovo. [In English]: "Displaced Kosovo Albanian refugees have settled in other parts of Kosovo reportedly without harassment from the Serbian security forces. These examples stand in stark contrast to persistent reports from refugees arriving in Macedonia and Albania of serious human rights abuses committed in Kosovo. In the village of Stari in Northern Kosovo, hundreds of young Albanian men can be seen wandering around or sitting on the grass. At the beginning of NATO bombing campaign, the refugees fled their homes in Podujevo region. Police worked their way south towards Pristina where some of them were allowed to stay. Then, according to refugees, the police opened up a corridor for them, allowing them to move northward again. Some of them came to rest in Svetlje. The refugees say the security forces leave them alone even though there are clearly supporters of the Kosovo Liberation Army in their midst." [Interpretation] And then there's a quotation here. [Previous translation continues]... "[In English]: ... to sell us cigarettes, they said. Meanwhile, in the south, we were unable to find any evidence of the tens of thousands of refugees who NATO allege are being kept here by the security forces near the town of Urosevac. One Kosovo Albanian man told us he drove his horse and cart from his village to the town every day and has not seen large numbers of refugees in the area. He and his family continue to live in their village while Serbs live in the village next door. These stories stand in sharp contrast to the testimonies of massacres heard from many refugees arriving in Albania and Macedonia, and they suggest a far more complex picture of refugee movements in Kosovo and the behaviour of the security forces." [Interpretation] Is this your article, Ms. Rowland?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to verify absolutely word-for-word because, I don't know about you, Mr. Milosevic, but I can't remember exactly what I was doing on Tuesday, May the 18th, 1999, at 2123 GMT, but I recognise the general drift of it, and I would thank you for reading it out in court because it I think it presents an excellent example of how the BBC is objective, fair and impartial and has sensitivity in portraying what was an extremely complicated conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this your article, though?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I recognise parts of it. I would not be able to put my hand on my heart and swear that it's word-for-word correct because, as I said, you know, you're asking me about something which I wrote over three years ago. You know, if I had summoned it up from the BBC website myself, then I would be able to put my hand on my heart and say it was. But this is the first time you've read it to me and you cannot possibly expect me to remember word-for-word exactly what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will let you have this to look at it so that you can see it.

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. As I said, Mr. Milosevic, by and large I recognise the article and, as I said, I'm very proud of it because I think it demonstrates the example of how the BBC is impartial, objective, and always wants to tell all sides of the story and to reflect on often complex situations. So thank you very much for your bit of publicity for the BBC there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Rowland, when you occasionally say something that is true, that doesn't mean that everything that the BBC reports about is necessarily true. Perhaps you're an exception, who knows.

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that a question, Mr. Milosevic? I didn't hear a question, I heard a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the article.

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it looks familiar. It looks familiar, but I -- you know, it's three and a half years ago. This looks like my article, as far as I can say, but, you know, I can't say 100 per cent that it is word-for-word my article, but it looks like the article I wrote, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you were in Kosovo, and some of the things you reported about in the article, some were provided in reports that the other side didn't show, but it's all on tapes that you filed. Do you consider that, for example -- do you believe that, for example, in the case that you witnessed in the Dubrava Prison, do you consider that the aggressor was the one who carried out the crime there by bombing the prison where you yourself said there were 1.000 prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That -- the view of the witness about that, even if she has one, is irrelevant. It's a matter which we're going to have to determine, as to what happened in Dubrava Prison. The witness can describe what she saw and heard but the conclusions from it are a matter for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She saw the prison in Dubrava, Mr. May, and that's why I'm asking her whether she assesses that the bombing of the prison is a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, a little while ago you mentioned that you were in Kosovo in the second half of May. Is that the only time that you spent in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I had the honour of holding a Novinarska Legitimacija signed by your Federal Secretary of Information, Mr. Goran Matic. I was BBC Belgrade correspondent from October 1998 until January 2001. During that period, I visited Kosovo on a great many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And during those numerous visits, as you say, who did you receive your information from on the locations that you visited?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking -- are we talking specifically about time spent in Kosovo during the NATO bombing or are we just talking about any times between October 1998 and January 2001 when I visited Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During the entire time, your experiences.

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: A great many people --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All the time. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: A great many people. Mr. Milosevic, as you're probably aware, journalists consult all manner of people from government ministers to simple villagers, farmers, women, children, men. We at the BBC are as interested in what ordinary humble people have to think about situations as we are about what ministers and government officials have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And please tell me, were you able to move about Kosovo safely?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depended on the time. There were times in Kosovo in the autumn of 1998 and the spring of 1999, obviously, when there were military clashes going on between the forces of the Serbian police and the Yugoslav army and the forces of the Kosovo Liberation Army when there were certain risks involved, certainly as journalists, in moving around the territory of Kosovo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the authorities enable you to go wherever you wanted or did they prevent you from going and making your reports? Did you have freedom of movement expected by a journalist?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the earlier part of the conflict, we enjoyed considerable freedom of movement. However, I have to say that in the days and last few weeks leading up to the NATO bombing campaign of Yugoslavia, our ability to move around in Kosovo was severely curtailed by the Serbian police and the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you report about the suffering of the Serb and other non-Albanian population as well as Albanians who were killed by the KLA? Did you report about that?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Milosevic. As you yourself have seen; balanced, impartial, objective, fair reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is a Serbian proverb which says that one swallow doesn't make up spring, so please do not generalise regarding this one objective report with the reporting of the BBC in general. Did you report about attacks by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Ms. Rowland. The comment is about a Serbian proverb about a swallow not making a spring, and it's said that you are trying to generalise from one objective report. Would that be right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I really don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What the accused is putting to you is that the BBC were not necessarily objective. That here was one objective report; the fact that there was one objective report -- at least, this is how I understand the point: The fact that there was one objective report doesn't mean that all the reports were objective. Since that point has been made, perhaps you'd like to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I take a great deal of pride in the reporting that I did from the former Yugoslavia, from both Bosnia, Macedonia, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as was including Serbia, the province of Kosovo, and I think that anyone who knew me in Yugoslavia at that time, including Kosovo Serbs, would say that I was one of the fairest and most objective reporters that they knew. For example, a few days before the NATO bombing began, a radio feature which I made was broadcast on the BBC on the Today programme on Radio 4, in which I looked at the issue of the demonisation of Serbs. And in my report, I interviewed a great variety of Serbian people about how they felt about the way in which their race was being demonised. I think that provides --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Rowland, as I understand it, there is no challenge to your personal objectivity. The question that is being raised relates to the objectivity in general of the BBC for which you work. That's what I think you should comment on, so far as it is significant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, A, I would question the significance, but B, I am very happy to say that the BBC enjoys probably the best international reputation of any broadcaster for being objective. And I should point out that during the NATO bombing campaign, Mr. Milosevic, as you well know, the British government was sharply critical of the BBC's coverage. I think at one stage some government officials referred to us as the Belgrade Broadcasting Corporation. They felt that some of our coverage, particularly some of the television reports filed by my senior colleague Mr. John Simpson, were too sympathetic to the Yugoslav viewpoint. So I think that all of this is proof, if any proof really be needed, that the BBC is an extremely objective and responsible international broadcaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you are proud of your reports, and as far as the one that we saw here, you have grounds for that, there is no doubt about that. We have to grant that to you. I didn't see that one, unfortunately. Could you please tell me, except for this report from Istok, did you report about the other consequences of NATO bombarding? Did you tour the towns and cities throughout Yugoslavia which were bombarded by NATO; civilian targets, hospitals, schools, buses, trains, moving trains, columns of civilians, people on bridges? Did you report about all of those things, Ms. Rowland?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself and my colleagues, yes. I should point out that at that time in Yugoslavia, we were a team of three BBC reporters; myself, Mr. John Simpson, who I just mentioned, and also Mr. Michael Williams. There were three of us, and between the three of us, we reported broadly on all the various things that were hit by NATO bombs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that you filed many more reports and taped more material than was actually broadcast. Do you think that in the choice of the material that was broadcast, the objectivity was reduced regarding the things that you were reporting about?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would doubt that very much. I have to point out that it was not a BBC cameraman who filmed the material. It was a cameraman from Antena Television. The Serb authorities were keener to have Greek journalists in Kosovo at the time than they were other journalists. I was something of an exception. The way it worked from a technical point of view was that the material which was filmed by the Greeks, they were kind enough to film a piece to cameras, as we saw. I would then give the voice track, which would be recorded onto a cassette. All of this would be taken by car to the border, to the Macedonian border, where journalists on the other side would pick up the tapes - so the visual footage and the voice track - and it would be physically assembled by a picture editor in Skopje, Macedonia. I obviously couldn't be there because I was not at liberty to wander in and out of Kosovo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that on several occasions you received information from, as you call it, the Serbian media centre in Pristina, which was known to you as an independent media source. You state this on page 2 of your statement. I assume that you remember that. Did this media centre provide you with correct information?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a great deal of respect for the media centre. I don't call it the Serbian media centre, I call it the media centre. I think the adjective "Serbian" was added in the statement so there shouldn't be any confusion. The media centre was run by Mr. Miki Mihajlovic, and Mr. Radovan Urosevic, and I think they did their best to do a serious job of collecting information and checking it, and the information that they gave I generally found to be accurate but not necessarily complete. I think they did their best to double-check their information from their sources in the VJ and the MUP, but I wouldn't have been able to go to the media centre to ask for information about things that were happening on the Albanian side, the Kosovo Albanian side. We used to go to other sources, including KIC, the Kosovo Information Centre, to get other information to complement the information that I was getting from the media centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to the prison. Do you know that in the prison itself, before the bombing and during that event, there was no military unit stationed there, there were no weapons, and that no military facility was stationed there nor any military unit was stationed in the prison? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I would have absolutely no way of knowing what the situation was at the prison before I visited because the first I even heard of Dubrava Prison in Istok was when we were taken there on Friday, the 21st of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it clear to you that this was a civilian facility since this was a prison that was being bombed?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have no way of knowing for certain exactly what applications the prison was being used for at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For what purposes can a prison be used other than as a prison?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's just a matter of argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see, then, or were you informed that during the bombing the deputy warden of the prison was killed? He's an Albanian. That some guards were gravely wounded, guards and other prison employees, as well as prisoners? Were you informed about that at the time?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, Mr. Milosevic, and I included it in my radio reports, in the radio reports that I filed on Friday, the 21st of May, 1999, which you can also find on the Internet if you care to hunt them out. I stated quite clearly that we were informed by officials at the prison that both inmates and employees of the prison had been killed and injured by the NATO bombing attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Rowland, do you have any doubt that those prisoners were killed by NATO bombing? Is there any doubt that these people were killed as a consequence of the NATO bombing? Is there any possibility that they could have been killed by something else?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are referring to my second visit to the prison on Monday, the 24th of May, 1999, yes, I have strong doubts that all of those prisoners were killed as a direct result of NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you very well. So there is no doubt that they were killed by NATO bombing or in your mind you do doubt that they were killed by NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On what do you base your doubts that they could have been killed by anything else other than the NATO bombing? When you see the dead people, what was it that could have killed them other than the bombing?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that some of them were killed by the NATO bombing. However, it was my assessment that some of them may not have been killed by the NATO bombing, and the reason I have those doubts is because of the appearance of the corpses. If a person has been killed as a result of bombing, I would expect to see some kind of injury on the corpse consistent with that manner of death. I mean, if, for example, I look at you now, Mr. Milosevic, I can see that you have both your arms, I can see the features on your face, I can see that your body is intact. If, however, you were hit by a bomb, Heaven forbid, I think I would be able to tell by looking at your body whether that was in fact the manner of your death. And the bodies that I saw in that second report, the bodies - which, incidentally, you didn't play the second report, I believe - the bodies that we see piled up in a room, a room that was not really damaged at all by the bombing, I have serious doubts that those prisoners were killed as a direct result of bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were collected there, there's no doubt about that. But do you know that the majority of people during the bombing are killed by the blast effect, that the bodies are not dismembered, their limbs are not torn off, or their heads. Death simply occurs because of the blast.

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bodies also, as far as I recall in that room, were not -- I would have thought if they had been involved in a blast, they would be covered with either dust or debris or plaster. I didn't recall them being covered in those. I'm sorry that I'm not a forensic scientist, Mr. Milosevic. I realise today that it was a regrettable decision to become a journalist, but I can only base my assessment on what I as a layperson, an observer, a firsthand eyewitness assessed the cause of their death to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact from the official report by the investigative judge that you actually talked to that, from the rubble, 93 bodies were pulled out? The report was completed after your second visit, as far as I can recall by the dates. We looked at it yesterday. But it does state in the report that 93 bodies were pulled out from the rubble, from the prison.

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that report, Mr. Milosevic, and for the record, your authorities expelled me from the territory of Yugoslavia a few days after I filed that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you willing to look? I provided photographs yesterday of the prison. So would you be willing to look not at all of them but only at those which depict the prisoners who were killed? The photographs were taken in the prison after the bombing. Would Ms. Rowland be willing to look at them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see the photographs. Mr. Milosevic, your time is practically up, but the witness can look at the photographs and you can ask some questions about it if you want. Yes. What do you want to ask the witness about the photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you notice that there are no dismembered bodies there but these are people who were obviously killed in the bombing?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say some of them look in a pretty bad state, Mr. Milosevic. This one here looks pretty dismembered to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that during your second visit you determined that the prison was practically razed to the ground?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not razed to the ground, Mr. Milosevic. We shouldn't exaggerate. Buildings were still standing. The building had been heavily bombed by the time I visited on the second time. It had been significantly damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you've had more than your time. You can have one more question, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the organs of the authorities continued with the investigation on the 25th when they also photographed, also sketched the place where it happened? They carried out the external examination by -- of the victims. This was done by doctors from Pec. Fingerprints were taken and other investigative actions were carried out and all of this is documented in records held by the District Court in Pec?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the details of the investigation because, as I said, Mr. Milosevic, unfortunately, your authorities chose to expel me shortly after I filed the last report we saw. Otherwise, I would have been very pleased to have continued to cover the investigation into the events of Istok prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. No. You've had your opportunity. Now, have the amicus any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just a few questions for you, Ms. Rowland. Looking at the material that was taped, I didn't see in the material any tanks in the prison or in front of the prison. Was there a tank or were there any tanks in front of the prison or within the prison compound?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that there were any tanks in or around the prison compound on that particular -- during the days of my actual visit. I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any in front of the prison? Were there any destroyed tanks or cannons or were they undamaged? Did you see that or did you perhaps tape that?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I do not recall whether I saw any tanks or not. You know, this is three and a half years ago. We didn't see any pictures in my footage, but I do not recall whether I saw any, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps you didn't see everything, but I would like to know about the wall that surrounded the prison. Was that damaged anywhere? And if it was and if you saw that, could you please tell us the extent of the damage.

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've seen the pictures, both on the video footage and the photographs which Mr. Milosevic kindly supplied. There was significant damage to parts of the perimeter wall. A segment two, three metres maybe was blown away, and there was also something of a crater in the ground below the perimeter all as well. So the wall was gone and there was a crater in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And also this: You stated that in your statement - it's on page 3 of the English version - you said here that the second time you visited the prison, you saw approximately 44 bodies of persons who were killed and that they were mostly covered with blankets. That means that you were not able to see the bodies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct, yes. We were not, as I explained in my statement, we didn't have a lot of time at the prison, we weren't at liberty to inspect individual bodies. I was counting corpses that were covered by blankets.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In a building, there were 25 bodies piled up; is that right? And then you add the bodies looked whole. They did not look as if they were blown apart by a blast. So there were no external injuries on these bodies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see, yes. That's correct, yes, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: May I? Ms. Rowland, you said that you had --

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No problem. You had strong doubts as to whether the bodies were all killed because of the bomb at that time. But you didn't mention that aspect in your statement. Why was that? Because it would be a very important aspect.

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which statement are you talking about? Are you talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The statement given to the OTP, the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have something along those lines there. Hang on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mentioned they are brought in, they might have been brought in, but you didn't mention that whether they are killed during the bomb or not.

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not there. I would say, as far as my television reports went at that time, I was only really at liberty to pose a series of questions. It was not clear how they died. It was not clear because, as you're probably aware, we were subject to censorship by the Serbian authorities at the time, but despite having been quite careful in what I said, I was nevertheless expelled two days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. And could you tell us more about your expulsion. Why was that? Was it because of your report?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never used to give me reasons for expelling me, although they did like to expel me on a number of occasions. They generally wouldn't give you reasons. Just when you would go to the foreigner's section of the police to renew your visa, which is an ordeal we had to go through on a weekly basis, you would just be told that your visa wasn't going to be renewed that week and you had 24 hours to leave the country. It happened on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did there come a time at a later stage that you came to hear of the massacre which had allegedly happened during -- between two of your visits to Dubrava Prison?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it later, yes. It would have been August 1999 that I heard about that. I was back in Belgrade by then. The Yugoslav authorities had seen fit to let me return and carry on my work in Belgrade. And I did hear about it. I was contacted by a number of colleagues who were in Kosovo at that time. This was after the NATO forces had moved into Kosovo following the withdrawal of the Yugoslav army and Serbian police, and a number of colleagues contacted me to tell me about I believe these shallow graves that were found and about the investigation that was going on, and they asked me to describe -- well, rather as I have done today, they asked me to tell them about what I remembered of my original visits to Dubrava Prison in May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you produce any report regarding that incident?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about in August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, no. One of my colleagues, Ms. Ola Gerin [phoen], did. She was one of the television reporters who was in Kosovo in August 1999. I was in Belgrade. I spent that period in other parts of Serbia, not in the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could tell us your opinion or assessment as to what happened regarding the alleged massacre, if you could.

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have sufficient overview really to do that, I feel. All I can talk about is the events that I witnessed at Dubrava Prison, and I think I've already described those in quite a bit of detail today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Half a dozen questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man in green civilian clothing, carrying the Kalashnikov and the pistol in the first report, was he apparently impeded in any way by the other people in the prison who were in uniform?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that I have no recollection of the movements of this man. He appears in my television footage but I have no personal recollections of anything he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused has raised with you a report said to be of yours and which you recognise in part in which you speak of the testimony of the massacres given by refugees in Albania and Macedonia. Did you speak to such refugees yourself?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a position to speak to the refugees in Albania and Macedonia because I was in Kosovo and in other parts of Serbia at the time. However, plenty of my BBC colleagues spoke in great detail to those survivors, and I think everyone is very familiar with those television reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The media centre, you describe its independence. You explain how you had to go elsewhere for material in relation to Albanians. Was the media centre loyal to a cause however carefully it checked its facts?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite clear that Mr. Miki Mihajlovic and Mr. Radovan Urosevic were there to present and defend their views and to defend the position of the Serbian people. Certainly they had a position, and yet I felt that they did carry out their work in a fair and honest manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The opinion you've given today about the pile of bodies as opposed to the bodies that you saw on the first occasion, is that an opinion - yes or no - that you've always held?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've always held that opinion, yes, from the moment I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Kwon asked you some questions about your statement. You interpreted his question as a reference to the footage. Maybe His Honour was asking about the written statement, but it doesn't matter. In the statement, you set out all the facts that you find, the bodies being intact, not appearing to have been blown up and so on. You didn't venture an opinion there. Was your statement a statement of fact?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was intended to be a statement of objectively observed facts rather than my layman's assessments, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: An opinion, of course, you were asked by the accused in the course of today.

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you see anything in those bodies that you saw from the position you did to indicate that they had been the subject of bombing deaths?

utterances.speaker: JACKY ROWLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I did see, and I remember particularly strongly and was quite disturbed by was the fact that, for some reason, their trousers were pulled down around their ankles, exposing their underwear, and that was very strange, I thought, and quite disturbing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Rowland, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I want to deal with some administrative matters next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two matters to be dealt with. The first is the next witness, Mrs. Imeraj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Her evidence is on a new topic and therefore should be given live, but obviously, given the circumstances, it must be dealt with in a very appropriate way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll deal with it in what I hope is an appropriate way. It may be that it would be not inappropriate for me to lead on a number of matters where I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have to say that there is a video of the deaths, and we have to bear in mind the wholesale challenge that's coming or that's been advanced to all these witnesses by this accused. There's a video of the family. It's a disturbing video. The witness has seen it. She wishes you to see it. I'll show it to her at the end. We'll show it in an abbreviated form by having one of the investigators in the booth fast forwarding it, if that's an acceptable course to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The other matter which I wish to deal with concerns the report which we've had on the health of the accused, which I trust has been seen by the Prosecution and the parties. It has been filed but it's right that I should deal with it generally now. We have this cardiological report concerning the high blood pressure of the accused. The doctor advises that sufficient rest periods for the accused be incorporated into the conduct of the trial as a result of the high blood pressure and recommends a period of four consecutive days every two weeks of trial. That is advice which we think should be followed not literally but as far as the spirit is concerned. We will consider, this week, a suitable programme which incorporates it as far as possible. We will sit this and next week and into a third week, if necessary, to try and finish this part of the Prosecution case, but we will consider if a break is required during the third week. We should consider, as should the parties, the overall effect on the trial as a whole of this new state of affairs and the progress which can be made. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond now to that with just these observations?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Assuming my calculation is correct and the remaining witnesses take less time rather than more time this week, but I'm not always very accurate, maybe I'm being over-optimistic, but nevertheless my calculation is that we may well not require the third week at all. There will, of course, be some outstanding issues and witnesses, and I'm going to have prepared for you by the beginning of next week a written document which we will file, setting out the position about all outstanding witnesses. Some of that may have to be ex parte, but we'll see. So I'm optimistic that we may be able to conclude by Friday week. May I call Mrs. Imeraj?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I respond to what we've just heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you may briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite briefly. First of all, I wish to emphasise once again that I did not ask for any examinations, and I did not ask you for anything. That is one point. Secondly, in relation to what Mr. Nice has been saying, what I'm going to challenge and what I'm not going to challenge, he does not know about that. Yesterday Mr. Nice explained here that I am challenging whether somebody is dead or not. It's not a question of challenging whether somebody's dead or not. It's a question of challenging how the person who is dead became dead. I am challenging the following, and I assert that, and anybody can see that, and everybody in Yugoslavia knows about that, that there is not a single officer or a single unit of the army, of the police, that would carry out an execution. So that is what I'm challenging. I'm challenging an execution, and whether somebody made a list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. This is not the occasion to expound on your case. Now, you've made your point. Now, I'm sure you'll bear in mind with this next witness the circumstances and take it into account when you come to cross-examine her. Yes. We'll call --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the next witness, I wish to object in principle. I am not asking. I am not requesting. I am not begging you for anything. I'm just asking you to put an end to the following practice: Last night around 6.00 or whenever, somewhere around that time, my associate Mr. Ognjanovic received a telephone call in order to be made aware that there is an addendum, a correction to the testimony of that witness and there are 18 points in terms of correcting her testimony, and that is what I am being given a day in advance. I'm not asking you to postpone the testimony of this witness, but what I do ask you to do is to put an end to this kind of practice on the part of this other side because this is impermissible. She gave her statement on the 9th of May, 1999, and they give me corrections this morning, because of course during the night my associate cannot come to the prison and bring me these corrections. And these corrections have to do with substantive matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us clarify this. What is the position here, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused has been provided with the addendum that follows on the proofing session with this witness, and the alternative is that she can give evidence and give all these matters without any notice, in the way that happens in most other trials because they're mostly matters of detail, or because the Prosecution attempts to help him and is scrupulous in its fair conduct in this case and have advance notice of matters that are a little different or need correction. It has been the policy I've pursued from start to finish, and the characterisation of the accused is extravagant, inappropriate, and entirely without merit. The addendum is designed to help him and you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Let's hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And while she's coming in, the Court might like to take the map at page 5. We just lay it on the overhead projector for those viewing. I don't think she's going to be looking at it in any great detail, but Padaliste is shown on page 5 at block L12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us your full name. And while that's being done, just for the purposes of spelling by any journalists, would the usher just lay this on the overhead projector. Your full name, madam.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: My name is Lirij Imeraj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Imeraj, you used to live in Padaliste?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your husband, mother-in-law, and nine children?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't want to take you through this in any detail. Are you in a position to tell us -- I may ask you some questions about this a little later. Are you in a position to tell us about how life for Albanians in your part of Kosovo changed in the course of 1998?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Albanians had a very difficult life in Kosova. We were persecuted by the Serbs, killed, beaten. Everything happened to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were checkpoints set up in your part of Padaliste?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: They put up checkpoints at Rakosh Hill, Cerkolez, Banja, all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you leave your house for a period in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Between what months?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: In August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Returning in?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: In November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving on just a little: Did you continue to suffer interference or attacks between November and the spring of 1999?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: A lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In particular, what happened on New Year's Eve 1998/1999?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: In 1998/1999, there was a lot of hail of gunfire at our house, shell-fire. We were never able to go out in the yard or even out into the meadow. We all had to stay inside in the cellar. This all came from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving on into 1999 and in particular to March of 1999. On the 25th of March of 1999, was there an attack that you can remember? An airborne attack.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, was there an airborne attack of which you can remember?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: There was in 1998, not 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. What was the date?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but it must have been round about August 1998, because that was when Padalishte was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From what airborne plane or otherwise was it shelled?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: It was a plane. It was a bomber. It belonged to the Serbs. The forces took off from the prison and bombed Padalishte.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What prison are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Dubrava Prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we see from the map with which we are familiar, Padaliste is not such a distance away from Istok and the Dubrava Prison, is it?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to the 27th of March of 1999.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: In fact the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that day, were you at home in the area of Padaliste that bears the same name as your family name, Imeraj?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: That's right. We were all at home, all our family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you become aware of Serb forces? If so, at what time and whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Serbian forces came in the morning, and we didn't notice them at all until they surrounded our house. And when we saw them, they were 50 metres away, and then they started to shoot. And we woke our four small children and put them behind the house to go out and flee with the children. And they were watching us, and they shot at the children. And Ardiana died on the spot and Afrim, five years old, fell. And I went out to see what was happening to the -- see what was happening to the children, and when I saw that Ardiana was dead on the spot and I went to Afrim and said, "Go inside." And the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter asks the witness to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Imeraj, can you slow down a little, and can I just interrupt your account to get a little more detail. We've heard that many, many houses of Kosovo Albanians are in the form of a compound with substantial high walls around them. Was your house in a compound? If so, was it surrounded by a wall?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: No. Our house was not surrounded by a wall. None of the houses in Imeraj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed, how many houses were there in the particular part of Padaliste called Imeraj?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: There were 18 houses in the Imeraj neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The troops who approached, did they approach just from one side, two sides, or from all sides of your house?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: On three sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The account you've given us so far of the children being shot at, before they were shot at, was anything said to them by the soldiers who were doing the shooting, that you could hear?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: After they came into the yard, they heard them -- I could hear them, and they were only 50 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they say anything or not before shooting at your children?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: After they killed Ardiana, they came up to the house and said, "Hands up because all the Beke family are going to die."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You described the family as the Beke family, that name being the name of -- that name being --

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: That's my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, let's pause there. A word or so about your husband. What job did he have?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: A teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where did he teach?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: He used to teach. He -- in Uca and in Lecina, Rakosh, and Susica, and 20 years ago in Bukosh.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What subjects did he teach?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Mathematics and physics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did he teach at schools for Kosovo Albanian children?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The soldiers who said that the family of your husband were to die, did you recognise the one who spoke or any of those with whom he came?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: They were in a group, and at that time I was -- I was scared. I couldn't really identify them individually because I was in a terrible state because there was my children and my husband in my house, and I couldn't really grasp what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time they first shot at your children, what if anything had your children done that might have caused them to be shot at by these men?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: The only reason was because they were Albanians, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at the time that they were shot, what were they actually doing? They were outside the house?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: At the moment when they shot, the four small children were in the yard. The others were asleep. One of them, I took off his blanket and said, "Get up." So they got up and we went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The ones who were outside, what were they doing? Were they standing still or were they moving away from the house or towards the house? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: My small son was playing, just like children do, in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After that first shooting, they came to the house. What did you do? You've told us about getting the one child up. Just carry on, please, with the account of what happened. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Half of the children I woke up. The other half were outside, playing, and I told them to go behind the house and flee and run away from the massacre. So I went in and I woke them up, and behind my back they killed my daughter and my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Then the children went out in the yard, and they were wounded behind, in the back, behind the neck, and I was wounded in two places and my skirt was torn in two places. And then the army came in and first they fired with automatic rifles inside the house, and the children fell to the ground, and then they -- then they entered. They threw outside -- they threw everything outside. My son was 15 years old, and I hid him, and I didn't see him any more. He was under the bed. I was behind the house, and I saw when they drew a knife on my husband and then I lost control, and I don't know how they killed him and I don't know with what they killed him. I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One minute. You'd got out of the house, you say, and you were at the back of the house. Were you able to hide yourself to some degree, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: After the house, behind the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hide behind something or in something?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Behind the house. And that house was in front and I was behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how did you stop yourself being seen? Were you just behind the house in the open ground or were you hiding behind something or in something?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: I barely saw them because I didn't go out to hide. I went out to protect my children. And then it was pure luck that I survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, when you get to a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That is as convenient as any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Imeraj, we are going to take a break now for 20 minutes. Could you be back at the end of that, please, to continue your evidence. Could you remember during the break not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that includes the members of the Prosecution team. We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Imeraj, I want you to conclude the account of what happened to your family members, and it may be helpful and swift if you do it in your own terms quite briefly and then I'll ask you a few supplementary questions on matters of detail. You already explained that as a result of what you saw you were obviously in a state of shock, but can you just try to summarise for us what happened to your children and your husband and how it came that you then left the house.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: The police, the Serb police, entered. My children and my husband were in the cellar. They took them by force outside the house. They killed them; six of my children, my husband, and my mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did they kill them? Was it with guns or in some other way or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: I mentioned earlier that I was not in a situation to see how they were killed, but I've seen them all fallen down, massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear any gunshots while you were there, apart from the initial time when they were firing at Ardiana?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear one burst -- was it one burst of gunfire or lots of bursts of gunfire or can't you remember?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Bursts of fire. There were lots of them. They didn't stop firing for maybe half an hour. They fired a lot. Bursts of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you leave the house and how did you leave?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: I was behind the house. I took my daughter with me, and I walked further up to see what had happened with the rest of the Imerajs. I contacted Nazmi. He was also wounded and asked me to help him with his wounds, and I told him, "Nazmi, I cannot help you. I'm here only with Arlinda." She was the only one who survived. All of my family was massacred. I was in a critical mental state. And I gathered with some others from the Imeraj family who had gathered near a stream. There were 13 of them. A little bit later, Albana and Feride, they also survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now that we've reached the stream, I'm just going to go back over the killing of your family and ask you for just a couple of matters of detail, if you can help us. The troops who came and did this, were they in uniform, and if so, what can you tell us about their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: There were people from the military, paramilitaries as well, policemen. There were lots of them. I couldn't even count them. There were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you notice anything about their uniforms, about what's called the insignia that they might have had on their caps or on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: One was wearing a black scarf around his forehead, and the others were wearing camouflaged caps. They had the Serb army and police insignia on their caps and on their armbands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, did you recognise any of these individuals yourself in the sense that you knew their faces? Forget whether you knew their names, did you actually recognise any of them facially?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Facially I could recognise them but I could not remember their names. We were surrounded in their checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say you recognise them facially, you recognise them facially as coming from where or as being where when you've seen them before? Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 9054 to 9060.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: From Cerkolez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What were they doing in Crkolez when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Well, a Serb, a certain Serb who they called Trajku, who used to come from Cerkolez all the time, our land was next to his. He was our neighbour at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was one of the men you saw?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: There were -- repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he one of the men you saw, this former neighbour of yours?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. From Cerkolez. They were from Cerkolez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've told us something about how the family of your husband was going to be killed. Was that something you heard yourself or was that something somebody else told you about?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: No, I heard it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you told any other things by the children who survived, of what was said to them in the course of this killing?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. They said, "You come out here. Why didn't you want to be compact with Serbia? Why did you want NATO?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was it who told you they had said those things? Which one of your children?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Arben and Albana.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time you left on your way to the stream, how many of your children did you think had survived?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Only Arlinda, because I was holding her by her hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In due course, you discovered that two others had survived, namely?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Albana and Arben. Shortly after, Albana came out from the house and she survived together with my 21-year-old daughter Feride. And I saw her at 20 metres while she was approaching our area. She was walking around and then I just screamed, I called out her name: "Albana, what happened? Tell me what happened." And she said, "They killed them all, Mom, they killed them all. And Arben is still under the bed." Then I returned to the house. My house was on fire. I wanted to see for myself what happened to my son. It was just possible that he was killed as well, but I wanted to go to the house and check. Then my two daughters dragged me, and they begged me not to go and check on the house because they feared that I might be killed as well. My neighbours also prevented me from going back to the house. Two hours later, approximately, when they set the house on fire, the police were still checking for survivors in the house, but they couldn't see Arben. When Arben set off in the direction of the stream, they fired two bullets in his direction, but the bullets did not catch him. When he arrived, he asked me, "Is any from our family still alive?" And I told him, "Yes, myself and two of your sisters are still alive." And I took him with us, and four members of our family, we were all together. So they did not succeed in exterminating the whole family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can we just have the names of your children who died and their ages at the time, approximately or precisely. Feride, was she 21?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Flurije, 19; Violeta, 17 years old; Ardiana, 13 years old; Arijeta, 11 years old; and Afrim, 2 years old. My husband was 52, and my mother-in-law 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think that Albana survived because, in the process of being killed, Feride fell on top of her and thus shielded her; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll now move to the stream. Perhaps just before we do, although your house wasn't in the formal fenced compound, did it have associated with it a guest room or I think they're called odas within the --

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll return to the reason for my asking you about that later. At the stream, how many other people from the Imeraj part of Padaliste were there?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
