utterances.text: About 13. About 13 were there when we all got together. When we sat there for a few hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there, as well as people who were alive, some dead bodies in the stream?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: When we set off for a location further up, we saw many dead bodies. We met Gjylfidan Imeraj, 15 years old. She was lying near the stream with her eyes gouged out. She was screaming, and she died two hours later. Rab Imeraj was wounded. She had three bullet wounds. She lived for another three days, together with her brother-in-law who was also wounded and had some of his fingers and toes cut off. There were lots of wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you can give accounts, if asked for details, of Gjylfidan Imeraj you've already spoken of, Mona Imeraj, who I think was 72 years of age.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mus Imeraj, 55, who was wounded. Then Rab Imeraj you've told us about. And then Nazmije Imeraj, who was wounded. I think you saw her.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: I also saw others. Is it necessary if I mention all their names?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I think we've probably taken enough detail. While you were at the stream, did Serb policemen appear?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did they say?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: They came to the stream. Before they arrived to our location, they had gone to the location where Rab and Mus were. They took all their money, all their valuables. Then when they reached our location, they also asked for money, for valuables, and everybody who had something on, we gave it all. And then one said, "Let's kill them." And then another one said, "No. Leave them alone. Don't."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you identified or did you identify yourself as Beke's wife when the Serb policemen were there?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: No. They did not know that I was Beke's wife because otherwise they would have killed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You went from the stream to the hills or mountains?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: To the mountains. We went to the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whose advice was it that you should go there?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: We decided ourselves, because when we heard Musa saying that they were going to come in a short time and take us and massacre us, then we set off in a direction further up in the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you hear Musa say that? Do you mean at the time you've just told us about, when he was stopped by one of the other soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: That was after the Serbs came to our location. And when they left, then as we were walking upwards, Musa told us what had happened, how they looted all the valuables and money, and then we -- all the rings, and then we went further up in the mountain and sheltered ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the mountains, roughly how many people were there gathered together?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: About 22 or 23. I did not count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Later -- and were they all from your particular part of Padaliste? Were they all from the Imeraj community?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you move to another part of the mountains called the big field, Fushe e Madhe?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: That evening at night-time, at about midnight, struggling through, we managed to pass without being noticed by the police. And the following morning, we walked to Fushe e Madhe, where we stayed for another ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many people were gathered there?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: There were about 25 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. But were there other people from other villages there?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: No, only from the Imeraj community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then did you, in due course, leave the area and leave Kosovo indeed and go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: We stayed in the mountains for ten days and then we set off on foot in the direction of Montenegro. We joined the convoy, and with my three children, I crossed, I went to Montenegro, after three days of journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple of details of other events which you'd heard or that you'd seen. This is at the foot of page 4, I think, of the statement. Was there one particular death amongst the Imeraj family of a man called Hasan Imeraj and his son?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. On 26th of March, on the same day, they also went to the family of Hasanaj. The family of Abdyl and Hasan were together at that time. They took Fadil Imeraj, Hasan Imeraj, they took them outside and they executed them at the front door.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you told of things that were said by the father before that killing and his willingness to die in the place of his son?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Before they killed him, Hasan said, "Kill me. Don't kill my son. We are neighbours." Because they were neighbours in Cerkolez. And they answered to him, "No. We are not neighbours. We are here to exterminate you." They knew Hasan very well, and Hasan's daughter also knows them, and she can testify about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In total, how many members of the Imeraj community were killed?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Nineteen members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your son Arben, who, I think to your surprise, survived, he having been in the house, has, I think, been reluctant to talk to you about the detail of what happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: No. He didn't want to talk to me about details because he knew I was a mother and he didn't want to worry me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, did he tell you anything about what the troops had done by way of speaking or singing at the time of the killings?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: I've heard them singing myself. My son told me about this as well. They were singing in Serbian Croatian language. They were singing in Albanian. They were cheering each other for having killed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your house was on fire, you say. All of the house, including the guest house, or any part of the complex of buildings?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: The house was burnt because the oda, the guest room, was a little bit further, near the entrance. The children were killed in front of the oda.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear from others what happened to the oda in due course and whether it was used at all by the Serbs or not?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: They haven't used it. I don't think they have. I don't know how they could use it when the bodies of my children remained in that room for three months, unburied. For that reason, they couldn't have used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we return to that particular issue, I just want you to look at one document, please. Perhaps you'll look at this document, please, and tell us when you first saw it and in what circumstance. When did you first see this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher would be good enough to place the original on the overhead projector initially and then we'll put an English version on top of that so those viewing can see what we're looking at. First the -- no. The witness can keep that. Thank you. Just lay that on the overhead projector. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was found with Shaban Mani, a deceased person. It is a list of persons who carried out massacres in the municipality of Istok.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just there, Ms. Imeraj. Because most people read English rather than B/C/S, so can we now put the English version on the overhead projector while Mrs. Imeraj keeps the Cyrillic version. We can see in English, Mrs. Imeraj, that the document is actually dated the 27th of April, 1998. "At an extraordinary session of the association of veterans of the war of 1990," setting out certain decisions. And we then see a list of people. And on the second page, if the usher would be so good, we see that over the signatures of a Mr. Djordjevic and Asanin, decisions were taken about weapons, about a working war staff being linked up with a working war staff of the municipality, and various other matters. Now, if we come to the list, first page again, please, the document's dated April, 1998. Roughly when did you first see it, please?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: The first time I saw this document was three weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Shown to you by whom?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: By the wife of Shaban Mani, who has the original of this document. .

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And according to that person, the document was found where?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: The document was found in Shaban Mani's house. The Serbs had left it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see on the typewritten version, and better on the original Cyrillic version, that Zikica Belosevic has been underlined in hand and that numbers 21 and 22 have been annotated in hand as Guso and Guso's son.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you explain those markings?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: It was composed by Shaban Mani when he was alive. This person was a commander who ordered the massacre at Imeraj's community. And the others also participated in the massacre, and all these persons whose names are underlined --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there -- pausing there for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I must interrupt. It's difficult to understand the significance of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The list is a list that came to somebody in your community and has the writing on it that we can see. Now, we can see that somebody's named as Guso, number 21, and that's a handwritten amendment to the list, and you've spoken of somebody called Guso. Is this the same Guso of whom you've spoken?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know him, but they said that he took part from Djurakovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the Belosevic, is that a name known to you or not personally?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Belosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Belosevic, number 18.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Would you repeat this once again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 18, the name Zikica Belosevic. Is that somebody known to you personally or not?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Belosevic. I've heard his name but I do not know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the document can be of use only as a list found in the area setting out the facts that it sets out on its face. I'd ask that it be available produced for that reason but for no further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Cerkolez, there is a neighbourhood called Belosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me repeat that so it's on the transcript. The exhibit will be given a number and exhibited for the limited purpose for which the Prosecution put it in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 293.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Imeraj, you've spoken of your family, your husband and children, being left unburied for many weeks.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: For three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you seen this morning a video, an amateur video, taken of the house in which you lived --

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- showing --

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Distressing as it obviously is to look at such a video, are you happy for it to be shown to the Judges and to see it or would you prefer that it can be produced, as it could be produced, by a later witness? Would you rather deal with it yourself or would you rather it was dealt with by a later witness?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Let's see it. Let's watch it. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a colleague in the booth who is going to fast-forward the video, and I can then, I think, probably ask just a few questions at the end of that. We'll give the video an exhibit number at the end if it's produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the first body is the body of your husband; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other bodies that we're looking at, are they the bodies of your children and your other relations who died?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Fast-forward, please. Fast-forward, please. I think that's probably enough by way of demonstration of the video. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are those the bodies of your family members left lying for three months in the garden?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can that video be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 294.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Imeraj, will you wait there, please, and you'll be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's for you to cross-examine. You will bear in mind the particular circumstances of this witness, I am sure, in cross-examining her.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry that this witness lost her family. Because of that, I'm going to reduce my own questions only to those that seem quite necessary to me. However, before I move on to my questions, let us try to clarify some of the timing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The time frame, from the statement, as far as I can see, this event occurred on the 27th of March. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: 26th of March. And it was on your orders that all my family were massacred. So you shouldn't feel sorry for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This tape is the 24th of June, 1999. So this is three months later. So all of it stood the way it was for three months then.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: So what difference does that make? Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify the timing to see whether it was clear to me. You described an exceptionally savage and cruel crime. That is what you've described. In addition, I see at the end of your statement that you speak -- that you say the following: "Most of them spoke the Albanian language." Then you say that they sang. They sang in Albanian and in Serbian, that they congratulated each other and, generally speaking, that they behaved like savages. My question is the following: Mrs. Imeraj, do you allow for the possibility that these were not Serb policemen at all or, rather, that they were not Serbs at all?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: It's not possible, not at all possible. They were all Serbs, and they spoke Albanian better than we did. They were our neighbours from Cerkolez. They all speak Albanian. We know they were Serbs. I could recognise them, my daughter could recognise them; they were familiar faces to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say to you that, for me, it is really incredible that Serb policemen kill children, sing Albanian songs, cut fingers off, and so on. So that is what I'm asking you precisely, whether it is possible that they did something savage and cruel like that and then they sing Albanian songs and then they massacre children?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Of course it is possible. They were our neighbours. They spoke Albanian. As we speak B/C/S, they could speak Albanian as well. They did it for fun, to kill Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Imeraj, your husband was an intellectual, from what I can see in this statement, and he was a member of Rugova's party, the LDK; is that right? He was an activist of that party, a prominent member.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the members of the KLA liquidated a large number of prominent members of Rugova's party on the eve of the war, during the war, and after the war, after the United Nations came to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: It's not possible. All those that were killed were killed by your hand, by those who were in Kosovo, who were positioned by you in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that it is precisely members of the KLA that in 1998 and 1999 committed various atrocities precisely towards the Albanians? And they claimed the Serb police for that or the Serbs who live in Kosovo. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: This is not possible, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm asking you whether you know about that. And do you know that in such events the members of the KLA, in order not to be recognised, wore camouflage caps and masks so that they would be disguised?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: How can a KLA kill Albanian? They're Albanians themselves. They were there to defend their thresholds. They were not there to kill Albanians. This is nonsense. This is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There are many such examples, but I do not wish to burden you with that. Do you know that among the members of these units there were foreign mercenaries as well, Mujahedin, who mercilessly carried out the most cruel crimes possible? Actually, the savagery and the cruelty of the crime that you described precisely resembles them. It looks like them doing it and then singing about it after that. This identifies them. Did you ever give it any thought?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: I never thought about it, and it can't be true. They were Serbs from Cerkolez, those who committed the massacre in my courtyard. This is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I advise you to give some thought to that, although I have no right to give you any advice. Please let us just clarify one more fact: In this correction that I received this morning, you wrote that you were correcting the second sentence in the third paragraph of your statement, and your correction reads as follow: "[In English] Our house was surrounded. I could not see who was surrounding us. I found out later from a document that it was a local paramilitary group. The document from which I learned this information was found by the late Mani, Shaban, in an office." Et cetera. Please.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: This is not true. This might be a mistake of the interpreter. I could see them well, that they were the ones who surrounded the house, they were the ones who killed my children. They were Serbs. And as far as this document is concerned, I just discovered it three weeks ago. And as for the rest, I know everything by heart because I've seen it with my own eyes. I've seen them myself, how they surrounded the house. I was there behind the house. This is not something that I've heard about, this is something I've seen with my own eyes. They were from Cerkolez. They were from Gjakove. They were all familiar faces. Only four or five of them were not familiar faces. This is more than true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Imeraj, I do not wish to upset you by this. I just read to you what I received, stating what you had allegedly said when correcting your statement. And this was submitted by the other side this morning. I'm not claiming that this is correct. I asked you how come it was possible then that you found out only three weeks ago, when you saw this document, who it was that surrounded you? Because here you say that you did not know who had surrounded you. That is what is written here. However, if they put it wrongly, then it's their mistake and I'm not going to torment you any further with this. Another thing I just wish to ask you: In this correction of your statement, it says here -- again I'm going to quote to you what I received. You say that you speak Serbian. Unfortunately, I cannot quote this to you in Serbian because I received it in English. "[In English] I also wish to add that in addition to the words I heard Belosevic Zikica saying to my ..." [Interpretation] and so on and so on. You heard what Zikica Belosevic and others were being told. A few moments ago when asked about this list, asked about this document, as far as I understood you, you said that you did not know Belosevic.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: I've heard all these names while they were shouting at each other, calling each other by names in the courtyard. I could hear everything. I could see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they address each other by their last names?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: By names. By surnames. They were calling on each other as they were going down the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you see that it says here in this list that it was established and that it has as its task to protect all the citizens and all the attacks of the Serb -- on Serb property and on Serb citizens and all people with a patriotic commitment?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: The Serb citizens, not the Albanian citizens. They were defending their own people, the Serbs. It can be seen on the videotape. The tape talks for itself how civilians were protected, how my children were protected. This doesn't need a comment. You can see for yourselves how they acted and what they did. All the world knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Imeraj, it is not being challenged here that you lost the members of your family. I just wanted to clarify the point that you could not be certain, first of all, that they were policemen; and secondly, that they were Serbs at all on the basis of the entire description, and that is why I put these questions to you.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: I'm 100 per cent sure. This is not based on description. This is something that I've seen myself. This document, I've seen it three weeks ago only. And what happened, I saw it with my own eyes, and you cannot deny it. I can tell you that I've seen the Serbs with my own eyes, and I've heard everything myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The accused is quoting from, I think, corrections --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- that were made this morning. Those corrections, however, were not passed on to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry if you don't have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're coming your way. I'll make an observation at the end of the evidence about the circumstances in which they were made available to the accused and when. The addendum was, of course, in the 92 bis package, but the decision having been made, I'm sorry it didn't reach you independently. It was my oversight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, could you just bring our attention to the precise passage that you just quoted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to tell you, Mr. Robinson. It is the third paragraph, the third sentence. It reads: "[In English] At the time when our house was surrounded I could not see who was surrounding us. I found out later from a document," et cetera. You can see that now, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The point that the witness was making is that it was the local -- she found out it was the local paramilitary group, from the document. But in any event, we can read it. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other quotation I made was the third paragraph from the bottom, where it says: "[In English] I also wish to add that in addition to the words I heard Belosevic Zikica saying to my husband," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And a short while ago, the witness said she had only heard of the name but she did not know him. I wish to point out these elements that simply indicate the fact that the witness can be confused with regard to the perpetrators of this crime, which is beyond any doubt. So I have no intention of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in view of the tragedy suffered by Ms. Imeraj, I did not intend to ask her anything, had I not received this today. It was actually today, during the break, during the trial, I got this translated into Serbian, this addendum. I'm referring to the addendum. I would just like to clarify something that Ms. Imeraj did not say earlier on. This is the last paragraph of this addendum. The last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Imeraj, you said that the night before the attack on the village, a helicopter had fired about 100 grenades on your municipality. That was the night between the 25th and the 26th. One hundred grenades were thrown on the municipality and --

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: No. In 1998 -- no, no. This is not true. In 1998, the helicopter bombarded in Citak and in Padalishte. And in 1999, nobody bombed. This is not true. This is misinterpreted. It was in 1998, in August. I can't remember the exact date. Citak and Padalishte were bombed by a helicopter which took off from the location near the Dubrava Prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Imeraj, I'm not going to insist, but you said the night before the attack. That is literally what you said two days ago. That is what is recorded here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling the truth here. What you're saying is not true. It was in 1998. In 1999, there were no bombings, there were only massacres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Imeraj, just a couple of matters arising. It's been suggested to you that the KLA had something to do with this. Were there any KLA present in your area?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: No. At the Imeraj neighbourhood, there was no KLA. No KLA in the Imeraj neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Has there ever, to your knowledge, been any hint or suggestion or question raised in an investigation about whether the KLA had anything to do with this killing, this massacre?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: The KLA has nothing to do with this massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: More than that - and this is at page 3 of the statement - a suggestion of the accused is that this was something that happened at the time of the bombing by NATO. Did you discover - this is at page 3 of the statement, second to last paragraph - did you discover later --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Nice speak closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you discover later something of a conversation between Slobodan Petkovic and Shaban Selmanaj about what was going to happen to your family?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us shortly the circumstances in which you learned of this and what it was you discovered.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Slobodan Petkovic said -- told Shaban Selmanaj that, as you are working in three schools --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Slobodan Petkovic told Shaban Selmanaj that, "How can Beke continue with teaching? How can he go to work? We are going to massacre him and all his family." He was also a teacher, Slobodan Petkovic, who used to work in the same school with any husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What ethnicity is Slobodan Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: According to what you've heard from Selmanaj Shaban, how long before the massacre was it that Petkovic had said what he said?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know how long before the massacre it was. My husband was still working in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did he stop working in the school?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: My husband? He worked in the school until he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So sometime before he died, according to Shaban, who I think was the school cleaning man, there had been a warning by Petkovic, the Serb, of the death to come; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the man Petkovic, is he still in circulation, still at liberty?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. He is still teaching in Cerkolez. He is still in the teaching.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, just to clarify, you've named the man Belosevic. Just help us; was that a name that you knew before the killing or not?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Slobodan Petkovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I moved to another topic. It's my mistake. The man Belosevic, the man who's been -- he's on the list and the man you've been asked questions about, did you know that name before the massacre or not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters request the witness to move closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Belosevic. Belosevic is the neighbourhood in the village of Suhogerlle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's name you knew certainly as a location before the massacre.

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear the name used at all in the course of the massacre or not?

utterances.speaker: LIRIJ IMERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those are the only questions I ask of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Imeraj, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The statement and the addendum have been referred to. They should be exhibited together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Have we given a number to the video as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have. Thank you. Before I move to the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The statement and addendum, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have them, of course, in the 92 bis package, which is probably the most convenient way if you ... While that is being dealt with, can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's just have a number before we go on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 295.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I move to the question of the next witness, I, of course, will take as little time as I can to correct the various unfortunate things the accused feels it necessary to say from time to time on procedural issues, but this morning's outburst should not go entirely uncorrected. First of all, I explained why it's in his interests and benefit to have things like addenda, and I hope he will accept that. Whether he does or he doesn't, he declines, I understand, to accept material by way of fax transmission, either from us or even, it may be, from the Registry. We've been asked to communicate with him via the Registry and this material was available yesterday for faxing sometime in the middle of the afternoon. His associates with whom I have attempted to create a relationship that would assist the accused lack instructions to deal with this directly, either in relation to matters of this sort or in relation, of course, to matters of Rule 68 disclosure, as the Chamber will know from the reports we've filed, and these outbursts of the accused are designed to generate interest or sympathy elsewhere but don't reflect what this Prosecution is doing to try to bring this matter to a speedy conclusion. Can I move to the question of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I said at the beginning of the week --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Nice move closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's either this microphone or my volume. Perhaps I must turn the volume up as well. I mentioned at the beginning of this week I might ask you to consider taking Mr. Merovci out of order. The Chamber will recall that he's coming back simply to deal with a television broadcast which is about a minute long which the accused raised with him and in respect of which he gave some answers already. He's a witness I took -- I can't be here after the second break. The video itself is available, Mr. Merovci is available, he's flown in, and I wonder if the Chamber will consider taking him now. I obviously haven't proofed him. He's obviously, as it were, in the course of cross-examination. He's simply here to have the video played and to give his answers to the text which we do have in the form of a transcript for you. The transcript would take about one minute, at most, to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has the transcript been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It hasn't been disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not to you but it's been disclosed to the accused. Because the accused it was who said -- he'd got a copy of the video. In any event, it was he who raised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, would you have any objection to Mr. Merovci being called next?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only request for the tape to be played that I provided for you awhile ago because the tape of his interview at that time was not disclosed. And then he can give his comments on that tape, because no one has seen that tape except for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this another tape, a different tape to that which has been provided by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I gave you the tape at the end of the cross-examination of Merovci. I told him about his interview and his stance in that interview, and I said that I had the tape. I had received it on that day. And the next day, I provided it for you. So that is the tape of his interview by which I confirmed that what I said was correct. But that tape, since he finished his cross-examination and left, was never shown. So if he wishes to respond to this interview, and it's a TV interview in which he gives answers, the answers and questions are taped in their entirety, so I ask that the tape be played and then Merovci can respond to questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can you assist about this? The accused apparently provided a tape. We apparently have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, is the tape which you're going to produce a different one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it's the same, and the transcript of this was disclosed in draft as long ago as the 27th of June, the final version from CLSS much more recently, but the transcript -- it's a very short point and if we just play it, I'm sure that the Merovci --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But the accused must have his tape played if it's different. So perhaps during -- we will adjourn now. Perhaps somebody could see if there's any difference between the two and then we'll decide what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I may not -- I may be here, I'll see, because I have to leave sometime -- at 12.40, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can be here for 20 minutes, perhaps, to short that out for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now. We'll hear Mr. Merovci. We'll play the necessary tapes after the adjournment. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, you have been brought back on a very limited point which we will deal with probably first by playing a video. The -- would you bear in mind that you're under the same declaration which you took when you gave evidence earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is, as I've now discovered, that the tape produced by the accused had been the subject of a transcript within Registry, but the transcript had never found its way to us. I make no complaint about that, these things happen. It's a longer tape than the tape that we have, our tape covering just the last part of it. I gather the accused wants the longer version played, which is about 14 minutes or something like that. And so rather than quibble about it, no doubt that should be done. I'm afraid I won't be able to wait to hear all of it myself, but that can be dealt with by my colleagues. Comparing the transcript of the relevant part of the longer transcript and the shorter transcript, I'm not sure quite how full the translation is, or the transcript is, on the first version but we'll have to hope for the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would ask that indeed it be played and that the witness be given an opportunity to comment on it at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Before we do, you say you have a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have a transcript that the registry has had. We have a shorter transcript, which is only of the last couple of questions and answers, but it does seem to be more detailed in format than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us have that transcript too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll hand that in as well. It picks up from the second to last page, I think. Yes. Let the video be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: VOICEOVER: [Interpretation] "SEHOLI: You're talking about a peaceful solution, how can we talk about a peaceful solution to this? "MEROVCI: We know that President Rugova has -- wants a peaceful solution, that the way he has chosen is the way of peace. President Rugova remains firm in this position and is committed to making a temporary solution for the people who have left Kosova, and he is one of the few people that can do something to alleviate the situation and to make use of certain mechanisms. And first, President Rugova is in a good physical state and is alive, and I asked that he be provided with a telephone and that has been done. "SEHOLI: You're one of President Rugova's close associates. In the meeting with Milosevic, he met with various associates like Fehmi Agani, Idajet Hiseni, Drita Tahiri, Alush Gashi, and Dzemalj Mustafa. Milosevic made a commitment, as I said before. According to what I have heard, these people are in Macedonia, in Skopje, and some are in villages. "SEHOLI: Did you have an opportunity to see the consequences of the NATO bombings? And what about the casualties of Albanians caused by NATO? "MEROVCI: I have met with -- specifically with Lubisha Vasic, the member of the Provisional Executive Council, and Prishtina is not like the city that we know and love. We have seen the damage caused by the bombing in the city centre, and my own office was in the bank building, and I worked there for years. And I haven't worked there because I was sacked from my job. But I think the -- the question of the flight of the population is a very complex one. It is very unfavourable for all concerned, and that is why we say that bombing has caused people to move, but this argument -- there was a counter-argument. Why have Serbs from northern Serbia not run away from the bombing? So this is really a complex issue. But I think to an extent, in an implicit kind of way, the bombing influenced the flight of the population. "SEHOLI: But Albanians didn't run away from the bombing. "MEROVCI: That is a counter-argument that might be used, but on the -- I have said before that this is a very complex issue, and time will tell and proper analysts will look at it and say to what extent the bombing influenced the movement of the population. But the main point, I think, is that this a complex issue that must be examined over time. "SEHOLI: How do you communicate with these people and what about their food supplies? "MEROVCI: I was out with the -- on the town and met some Albanians, some friends, and they were pleased to talk with me because they had heard that Rugova was wounded, and they also heard some interviews on the radio. And I myself saw that the shops had -- had, to an extent, improved. I saw some shops were open and also some state shops, and they were open, and they had bread and milk, yogurt, and staple groceries. And I also heard that four kilos per head of bread were available. "SEHOLI: What about the talks that Milosevic started towards helping a solution of these humanitarian issues? "MEROVCI: After the meeting with Milosevic, the idea arose of continuing the political process with a -- to these severe problems, and we can talk about solving the issue of Kosova and alleviating it on the basis of the Rambouillet agreement. And it's a matter of bringing people back. And I would say that there are negative factors influencing the situation. "SEHOLI: What did you talk about with Mr. Christopher Hill, the US intermediary in Skopje? "MEROVCI: We used to have regular meetings and the talks were constructive, and he spoke to me on the telephone, and he asked me about what condition Mr. Rugova was in, about the situation in Prishtina, and other questions. "SEHOLI: A league for peace has been formed in Prishtina by the Democratic League of Kosova. Do you think that this will give a contribution to ease the atmosphere, and can Mr. Rugova be involved in this? "MEROVCI: Mr. Rugova is a major political figure. He had a meeting with Mr. Milosevic. You have to realise the circumstances in which he finds himself. I do not think it is worth giving too much importance to formal meetings and to photographs, but we have to do vital things to ease the present situation. "SEHOLI: This is the private television ASK in Albanian. Please tell our viewers whether this conversation we're having has been to order. "MEROVCI: First of all, people asked me whether I would do this interview and I agreed, and there was no pressure put on me. I am one of Mr. Rugova's staff, and I'm not subject to political obligations, and I would say there are no bad answers, there are bad questions. And I can say again I am not in the same position as you are, and I can say now in public that I do feel under a certain kind of pressure, and I don't need to say any more. "SEHOLI: Would President Rugova in this moment be in a position to address the people of Kosova? Because there's been a lot of rumours. He's been talking to people like Baton Hadziju and other close colleagues. "MEROVCI: As to the people you mentioned, I heard that -- I've seen interviews on television. I've heard that the person in question is abroad and -- we've heard that he's alive, Fehmi Agani, and we're trying to contact to contact him. We're trying to contact his family, his son, who said that he had information that his father was alive, Fehmi Agani. It could be true or not. "As to Mr. Rugova and his statements and interviews, he's not the person fond of making statements and comments and journalistic speculations. I remember his words quite well. Mr. Rugova has made several declarations, and he will speak again at the proper time. "SEHOLI: Difficult moment in our country. Perhaps not a great contribution but at least a moral contribution, moral assistance could be given, moral support by him. "MEROVCI: The reference of Mr. Rugova in Kosova and his presence in the public so that the public can be convinced that he will uphold the values you mentioned so that people will be more secure, feel more secure, and people will return. As I said earlier, some people I met, it's a fact that I've mentioned a number of times, the only inspiration in this situation is that the conflicts between the people, between the Albanians and the Serbs and between the people in general in the streets, I have not heard about. There's a lot of rumours about damage, but still, in this situation, there are a lot of people out of control, maybe from the Serb side, larger groups. "SEHOLI: Information from Croatian television. What would be your message for them? "MEROVCI: My message is what has happened has happened. We need not go any farther, because very soon the time will come that we will be able to return to our homes, where our houses were, their houses were. They can come back, and I hope my expectations are based on facts and not on fear and panic but on complete safety. "SEHOLI: To viewers, this was an interview with Adnan Merovci, protocol head of the President of the Liberal Alliance of Kosovo, Ibrahim Rugova. "Mr. Merovci, thank you very much."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, I was thinking about it. I think it's probably right that Mr. Milosevic should begin and you can re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Questions about this tape, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You received a transcript of the interview, which is a little more precise than the simultaneous interpretation. It was very difficult, I assume, for the interpreters

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there is no doubt that you, Mr. Merovci, in this interview, are in favour of cooperation, understanding you're pointing to the consequences of NATO bombing, and you also point to ways out in cooperation between the Serbian and the Albanian factor. Is this so or is it not so?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, that's not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In this brief extract from the interview which you gave, which takes up less than two full pages, you were asked whether you saw the effects of the bombardment and what you think about the attacks by the NATO forces and did they cause the movement of refugees. Your answer is that it's a complex question, that there are both of these issues. There is also a counter-argument because in the northern of Serbia Serbs are fleeing the bombing, even though it's a complex question, and then you say: "And I think to a degree implicitly the bombing influenced the departure of the population." So did the bombing cause the population to flee or not? This is something that you confirm here even in this answer of yours here.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: In my statement in May, at the end, you insisted that I have time to answer your question, and I would paraphrase. You said at the time that the main cause of the movement of people from Kosova was NATO bombing. That was your question. And my reaction was: No, it's not true. The situation was as it was, but this -- it was an interview here that was broadcast on terrestrial transmission, but it's not the whole interview, this tape. It was edited. It's only part of it. You can see that it's edited by my movement of my hands. I was surrounded. I was in front of the camera. There were soldiers around me, people armed, civilians who were armed standing around me. If you look carefully, you can see. You can hear their voices. So I want to insist that what I said and what I asserted there during the interview is true. What I said I did say and I meant. But one should take into consideration the special circumstances. The question as to whether NATO caused the movement of refugees, my answer in May, here at the Tribunal, was no, and you can see that in the material. I was -- during the television interview, I was standing in front of guns. You can't argument that the -- you can't take -- you can't explain the movement of the Albanians only. There were other people too who were fleeing. So why, then, were the Albanians going to Montenegro? Because, after all, there was bombing in Montenegro too. So the attempt to say that NATO caused the fleeing of the population is not true. There were Serb -- implicitly because Serb and Montenegrin forces were taking revenge for the NATO bombing. So I can repeat now that NATO was not the cause of the flight of the population, and I can comment in this way on the -- what I said in the video cassette.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Merovci. We don't want to exaggerate now. Are you trying to say that you condemned the NATO bombing in this interview because you had guns pointed at your -- at you? Is that what you're saying, that you condemned that because you were faced with guns?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: I have no need to demonstrate this because this is true and exact. You can ask the interviewer in this video cassette because he was in the same situation, even though he was one of your quislings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you yourself and this man - I don't know who it is, it's probably an editor of this private TV station - so you and him at gunpoint made this interview. And the guns were pointed by our forces. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: The room where the interview was held and behind the cameras that were filming, in this room there were four or five men who were working with their automatic rifles and were toying with them, and you can hear them on the video cassette. And you can hear their whispering and the noises they make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, please, Mr. Merovci. These are such unbelievable things that I really do not want to squabble with you about them. But let's move on to the material facts. You compare the bombing of Kosovo to the bombing of other parts of Yugoslavia. Are you aware of the fact that out of the total bombing of Yugoslavia, 40 per cent of the bombs fell on Kosovo and Kosovo comprises only 10 per cent of Yugoslavia's territory? That is to say that the bombing was four times more intensive in Kosovo than it was elsewhere? Do you at least recognise that fact?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: This can be shown by what I have said. The movement of Albanians from Kosova was not at any time caused mainly by the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that from Kosovo - again, from Kosovo - due to the bombing - and this is contained in the same UNHCR tables - about 100.000 Serbs and other non-Albanians fled in addition to the Albanians who fled? Are you aware of that fact? So they were fleeing from the bombing, the Serbs and other non-Albanian population as well. Why were they fleeing, then? Why were the Serbs fleeing if it wasn't due to the bombing of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't believe that that is accurate, and I said before and I say again, the movement of the Serbs has not been shown to be from this cause, and they didn't -- and I say it again, the Albanians didn't have reason to flee because of the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They didn't have reason? And do you know how many Albanians were killed by the bombing? And you yourself in this interview said that the centre of Pristina was destroyed, it was no longer the town that you loved, et cetera. You say that in that interview. And it so happens - this is a coincidence - today we had the opportunity of seeing a BBC report that depicted the destruction in the centre of Pristina, and it fully corroborates what you said. So these are facts, Mr. Merovci. And what do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: The question of the bombing of Prishtina, this involved only the old post office where your police and army forces were stationed. These are the men who caused massacres in the population. So NATO properly performed its mission by bombing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Merovci. I do not doubt your need to make propaganda speeches now in contrast to what you said before. However, in this excerpt that you provided, that is to say that you selected the excerpts that spell out in relative terms what you said in the interview, again, there is a question. As I go back to this interview, Serbs were fleeing from the north but Albanians were not fleeing from here either before the bombing. That's what I'm asking you about. We saw the transcript here on the monitor, but it was very difficult for the interpreters, so they were not in a position to interpret the interview fully. But it says it here in this transcript. "I said this is a counter-argument," et cetera. "But I think that the bombing influenced people to get on the move." That is what you say. So what do you have to say to that now? Is this your interview or is this not your interview?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: The movement of Albanians from the territory of Kosova started even before the NATO bombing, during the notorious offensive of the summer of 1998 and there was the movement of Albanians from destroyed villages. But during the NATO bombing, these movements were caused by your forces and by your platform of ethnic cleansing. And all the evidence so far supports this. And as for my interview, I gave it under the circumstances in which I found myself, and I am able to answer for everything I said in it. Certain buildings were bombed, and various buildings around were also damaged as a result of the bombing, but in the main building that was bombed, your forces were stationed. So I would say to your question did I give this interview or not, I would say yes, I did, it was in that month of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say that you gave it under duress.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: If you want to dwell on this point, I will explain that this interview -- that I was forced to give this interview, in fact. This interview, the request was to have an interview with Mr. Rugova, and I agreed to give it. But its purpose was merely to make a statement in -- to the world to provide a comment about a comment by a German journalist on a news programme and -- and I was surprised by the argument. An interview without discussing it in advance, making a declaration; these are conditions which I accepted to -- under which I accepted to make the interview, to do the interview. But there were other questions which were not on the tape. The interview was not broadcast for three weeks. They probably didn't like my answers, that's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me clarify this: Who was it who requested the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, the request for the interview was made by contact people, people who contacted us. It could be the so-called secretary Mr. Vasic. And the request was for an interview with Mr. Rugova. The interview was carried out in an ad hoc -- at an ad hoc studio, it was typically political -- politicised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic at the time presented himself as the secretary of administrative affairs in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In answer to Mr. Milosevic, you just said that you were forced to give this interview in fact. So by whom were you forced or by whom did you consider yourself to be forced? Was it by Mr. Vasic or by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to go back too far. It was a continuation of other declarations I had made. At the time, we were under arrest, we were hostages, and everything that we did was to save our own skins. And in this context, we were asked for a comment from Mr. Rugova for -- about the article in the German paper Der Spiegel. At first, Dr. Rugova refused and said, "What have I got to comment on?" but later they insisted and he asked that I should, in a way, make this comment because I was his sole close colleague. And I considered myself obliged to make this comment, considering all the circumstances that I gave in my evidence, and when I went downstairs, instead of seeing a camera and a microphone, I met a person who spoke Albanian who I didn't know, and he said, "We're going to make an interview." And I was confused. And behind the cameras, I saw armed men. And I, as an intellectual, realised that this was a moment where I had to accept this interview, and I think this contains the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's important for me to understand it and, I could imagine, for the Chamber. In the transcript, you're asked by Mr. Seholi to say if the interview has been imposed or ordered or whether it is the expression of the will for surmounting the crisis, and your answer to that was: "I have accepted it, and I declare under my full responsibility that I have accepted it without any pressure, because it is not in my nature, in the first place, because I am just an activist involved not in politics but in service." So that in the interview you declared that you were not under any pressure, you were not forced, but now your explanation is that you were in fact forced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my answer was that I had been forced, I wouldn't be here today. And you can see from the transcript that I say that nobody is free in this situation, nor was I. So I can tell you that I was a hostage, I was under arrest, and then you can understand everything. And we went to Belgrade, and we did make certain journeys. And from this you can understand that we were hostages and under arrest. So we weren't in a situation to refuse. And you can -- you can understand now what the accused is driving at, but the facts are here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The physical situation in which you were placed that made you feel that you were a hostage, explain a little more the physical surroundings, the soldiers who were there and the situation as a whole that led to your considering yourself a hostage at that situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, I must say that I have seen this video material. I have seen the copy. I viewed it. And the copy shows very clearly, although the monitor in front of me was not very good, and first you can see on my face various consequences of some ill-treatment I suffered earlier. Second, the noises off and the sounds of the weapons that were being moved behind the camera, you can -- in the video version, the original one which I have here and which is the same but which is an earlier copy, you can hear these noises off and the noises of the automatic rifles and also my own movements and the way I'm looking in the interview. And if you watch it carefully from the beginning and if you look at my appearance at certain critical moments, you can see that I am looking at the armed men behind the cameras who are moving their automatic weapons. And these are the circumstances under which I gave this interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you then saying that the entire interview, including your statement on which Mr. Milosevic relies that implicitly the bombing caused the fleeing of the people, is to be understood in this context, in the context in which you were under pressure? Is the entire interview to be read in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My reply that the movement of the population can be implicitly ascribed to the NATO bombing, this answer was subtle in its own way in the situation in which I was, because to get by this moment, I had, in a way, to find a diplomatic answer. And in this word "complexity," this contains a lot of things, and thus I avoided saying yes or no and I gave a rather conditional and diplomatic reply to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, awhile ago you explained here quite unequivocally that you did that and that Rugova did that because you had to save your own skins. That's the way you had put it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And does it seem to you that actually by your purported denial now you are doing precisely that, saving your own skin from the KLA? And they loom above your heads, and you have to deny everything that is true and everything that you said in order to save your own skin today, under present circumstances in Kosovo? Is that right, Mr. Merovci, or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: There is not a -- there's not a single angstrom. You technician scientists will know what that means, but not a minute particle of that holds water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Merovci. You did not answer the question put by Mr. Robinson. Who was it who forced you, blackmailed you? Who threatened you, by what, and who was the person who forced you to give this interview? And what kind of threats were issued? Please answer both aspects of the question. Who threatened you and with what kind of threats?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: I explained the circumstances under which I gave this interview. And the request was for Mr. Rugova to make this statement, and I agreed to come out in his place because of my obligations to him as a colleague, but I can repeat that everything that we did was done on the basis of a general kind of duress. And my description of these circumstances shows and provides the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci -- just a second, Mr. Milosevic. In an answer to my -- to Judge Robinson's question, you mentioned that we can see on your face various consequences of some ill-treatment you suffered earlier, on the TV. Would you clarify that meaning to us in specific terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was physical mistreatment of me in May when my house was entered and occupied on 31st of March. And on my face, or the black eye - because I've got to give a real answer although I don't really want to answer this question - this interview took place on the 14th of April, and you can imagine that you can still see the consequences of an injury of that kind after that length of time. So if you look at the video cassette carefully and in colour and in the original copy of the video, you can see it, but you can't see it on this black and white copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you were beaten, were you asked to have an interview at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was when the troops entered the house and I was maltreated. But this event made me feel under arrest and gave me a sense of being a hostage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we cannot continue on this particular point much longer. We must to finish today. You've got another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please just give me brief answers. On the 31st of March, they beat you; right? You just said.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of April, you came to me with Rugova; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how come nobody noticed on the 1st of April no bruises on you nor that you complained that anybody had beaten you, and you say that 14 days later you still had bruises? Who can believe you, Mr. Merovci?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: I was asked this question in May, and I've already given the answer. You've got it on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you answer? You said now that on the 14th of April, you had bruises dating back to the 31st of March, and you didn't even have them when you came to see me with Rugova on the 1st of April, and you did not mention that anybody had laid a finger on you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What he said -- let me just read my note so it's clear. In cross-examination, he said he didn't complain to the accused - he must have been referring to the 1st of April - about his maltreatment because it was trifling compared with what happened to others in Kosovo. That was his answer in May.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he gave the same answer that he gave now, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you once again: When did you go to Italy with Rugova?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: On the 15th -- 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You left on the 5th of May. And then you were in a safe place; right? When you went to Italy, you were in a safe place; right? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: We were free men then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So then when you came to Italy, why did you not say on the 5th of May, on the 6th of May, on the 7th May, on the 10th of May, or the 10th of May the following year, Mr. Merovci, for that matter, why did you not say that you gave this interview under duress, that you were not telling the truth, that you were forced to do so? Why did you not say it then? Why did you not say it then when you were not speaking at gunpoint any more? This is the first time I hear that somebody has guns pointed at him in a TV studio and that he is giving an interview. Why did you not say then, "I did not give this interview. This interview was taken from me under duress"? Why are you saying it only now, three years later? You're saving your own skin from the KLA; is that right, Mr. Merovci?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a separate point. The first point you're being asked about, Mr. Merovci --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said about the KLA in May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Don't deal with the KLA. The question you're being asked is, first of all, why didn't you mention that the interview was given under duress earlier, for instance, when you were in Italy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interview -- the interview -- the question in the interview was what was the main cause of the movement of the population, and I gave the answer -- the diplomatic answer at that time. And now you ask me why this -- why I did not say that this interview was given under duress. But at that time, every gesture, everything I did, everything we did was done in the capacity of a -- someone who is under arrest, a hostage. And in the final analysis, the essence of the interview I cannot deny. I don't say I didn't say these things, but if I describe the atmosphere and the surroundings under which I gave this interview, then it becomes clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was it under this duress that you explained in the interview that life was going back to normal in Pristina, what we heard now, that there were better supplies in the shops and that there was enough milk, bread, yogurt, pastries, et cetera? Did somebody suggest that you say that as well, in terms of positive developments in Pristina and normal life taking place once again? Were these Kalashnikovs pointed against you because of yogurt?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you say that it was under duress that you explained that due to the NATO bombing, people were running away. Was pressure exerted against you because of yogurt as well, that you had to say that there was enough bread, milk, yogurt, et cetera, that life was being restored to normal? Did you do that at gunpoint as well?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: What I said is what I said and that's what it was like. If you want to analyse it, you should have gone to villages around Prishtina, gone to Pristina yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, I am saying that you did say what you said. I completely agree with that. But, please, could you please tell me, since you mentioned a little while ago how the person who made the interview, as well as you, were both under pressure. Does that mean that the questions were made up under duress or perhaps somebody gave him the questions he was supposed to ask. How was this interview organised? How did it come about for him to ask these questions since he was under pressure as well?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's a question you must put to him if he comes here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic that must really bring it to an end, but you can ask one further question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In spite of the fact, Mr. Merovci, that the people fled from NATO bombing, they fled as far as Albanians are concerned. They also fled because you called the people to leave their homes. You issued flyers and appealed to the people to flee, in order to justify the NATO intervention. We have to skip a whole series of questions in relation to this point, but since you and Rugova claimed here that you saw this pamphlet but it wasn't yours, why did you not, on your departure to Italy on the 5th of May say that this pamphlet was not yours if you felt that this pamphlet was a false one, the one calling on Albanians to leave for Albania? Why did you not say expressly that this pamphlet was not done by you?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: I will only ask -- answer the questions which involve me. Mr. Rugova can answer his own. And I will answer according to the -- about the pamphlet that you fabricated, there are a lot of evidence -- there's a lot of evidence to support what I said because on the first day when Rugova returned home from Paris, he -- he supported the NATO bombing. So it's not true that he was against it. Second, this pamphlet bears two names, the KLA and Rugova, and this does not correspond to the reality of the situation. And as for your question why we didn't declare this pamphlet a fake, the forgery was so transparent that we didn't see fit to deal with it. And nobody remembered this pamphlet until you reminded us of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to bring your time to a close. You've been examining for a long time. Yes. Re-examination on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm afraid we haven't time for your questions today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Merovci, last time when you were questioned and when the existence of this interview was mentioned, why didn't you say then that it took place under such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. There's no need to go into this. Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, Their Honours have asked most of the questions about what I wanted to ask you about in terms of background but I just want to be clear about a couple of things and then I want to ask you a particular question about the transcript itself. As I understand what you have said, that you were initially taken hostage on the 31st of March and then you went to Belgrade on the 1st of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Mr. Rugova went and so did I.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And you met with the accused. Did you remain in Belgrade for the next two weeks, until the 14th of April, when you gave this interview?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: No. We returned to Prishtina the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How is it, or where did this interview take place? I understand, sir, that this happened -- well, you tell us. Where did this interview take place? Was it in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: The interview took place on the ground floor of Mr. Rugova's home. He has a living-room, an entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. So the camera crew and everybody came to Rugova's home, is that correct, for this interview?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the translation. Yes. The team came to his home, but I'd just like to remind you that to get into Mr. Rugova's house you needed all sorts of authorisations, go through police post blocks and things.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did these armed men come with the camera crew or were they already in Mr. Rugova's home?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: The people I saw I hadn't seen before. The house was always surrounded. There were even armed people in the house and around the house, certainly. But as individuals, as far as I can remember, they were people who had come in especially for this -- for that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Prior to your attending this interview, were you aware that there were armed forces around and in Mr. Rugova's home?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Recalled]
utterances.text: During the interview, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
